title: Blood, nectar and fruit
teaches: Why vampire bats feed hungry roost-mates, how bats live on blood, nectar, fruit, fish and meat, and what nectar and fruit bats do for plants
summary: **Most bats eat insects, but not all.** Others live on nectar, fruit, fish, frogs, birds or, in three American species, blood.
**A vampire bat lives close to starving.** A bat that misses two nights' feeding in a row usually dies, about 60 hours after its last meal.
**Vampires find blood by heat and keep it flowing with spit.** Pit organs on the nose sense warm skin, and an anticoagulant in the saliva stops clotting while the bat laps.

**Vampires feed hungry roost-mates by bringing up blood.** Gerald Wilkinson found in Costa Rica that they give mostly to relatives and to roost-mates they know well, which are the bats likely to feed them in turn.
**A gift costs the donor fewer hours than it gives.** A full bat loses weight fast and a hungry one slowly, so the same few grams move the hungry bat much further from death.
**Paying back starves cheats.** In a model roost, a bat that never gives is soon fed by no one if bats feed only those that have fed them, while a rule of feeding everyone lets it take for free.

**Long-nosed bats carry agave pollen tens of kilometres in a night.** Wild agaves open their flowers in the dark for them; tequila agave, grown from clones and harvested before it flowers, is now rarely pollinated by bats.
**Fruit bats drop seeds in flight.** Birds mostly drop seeds where they perch, so bats are the ones that seed the middle of a cleared patch and start the forest growing back.

blocks.text: Hacienda La Pacífica was a cattle ranch near Cañas, in the dry northwest of Costa Rica, in the province of Guanacaste. In the late 1970s and early 1980s Gerald Wilkinson, a graduate student from the University of California at San Diego, spent his nights there with the vampire bats that fed on the ranch's cattle. They roosted in groups in hollow trees around the pastures. He caught them, marked each so he could tell it from the rest, weighed them, and then watched the roosts in the hours before dawn as the bats came home from feeding on the cattle.

Many came home heavy. A few came home light, having found no animal to bite or been driven off one. And sometimes Wilkinson saw a light bat lick at the lips of a heavy one, and the heavy one bring up blood from its stomach into the other's mouth. He saw it 110 times. Seventy-seven of those were mothers feeding their own young. The other 33 were between bats that were not mother and child, and some of those bats were not related at all.

A vampire bat has no fat to speak of, and blood is the only food it can digest. Every meal it gives away is food it may need itself tomorrow. So why give? And if a bat is going to give, to whom? Wilkinson's answer, published in *Nature* in 1984, is the centre of this lesson, and it turns on how a vampire starves, which comes first.

Three species of bat drink blood, and all live in the Americas, from Mexico to Argentina. The **common vampire bat**, *Desmodus rotundus*, weighs about as much as a large mouse, 25 to 40 grams, and feeds mainly on mammals: cattle, horses and pigs since Europeans brought them, tapirs and deer before. The other two, the white-winged and hairy-legged vampires, mostly feed on birds. No bat in the Old World drinks blood.

A common vampire usually lands on the ground beside a sleeping animal and walks, hops or runs to it on its wings and thumbs, as few other bats can. It finds a place where blood runs close under the skin with heat sensors in three small pits around its nose. In 2011 Elena Gracheva, David Julius and colleagues found what makes them work: the nerve cells serving the pits make a shortened form of a protein called TRPV1. The full-length form, in our own skin, makes us feel a burn at about 43 °C. The vampire's short form switches on at about 30 °C. Warm skin, at well over 30 °C, gives off infrared radiation, the warmth you feel on your face from a stove across the room, and that is enough to warm the sensors in the pits from several centimetres away.[^trpv1]

With its upper incisors, sharp as razors, it shaves away a little hair and cuts a shallow wound a few millimetres across. It does not suck. It laps, its tongue running in and out of the wound for twenty minutes or more, while its saliva keeps the blood flowing. The saliva carries several **anticoagulants**, substances that stop blood clotting; one, a protein described in the 1990s, was named **draculin**.[^draculin] A meal can weigh half the bat's own weight or more. Within minutes of starting to feed the bat begins passing the meal's water as urine, so that it can still take off.

Blood is mostly water and protein, with very little fat or sugar, so a vampire cannot build up a store. Wilkinson's weighings showed a bat losing weight after a meal until, about 60 hours later if it had not fed again, it fell to a weight at which it starved. It is the weight that kills, and 60 hours is how long an unfed bat takes to reach it. A vampire feeds around the middle of the night, so a bat that misses one night is about 48 hours from its last meal when the next night comes; if it misses that one too, it will not last to the third. Two missed nights in a row are usually fatal. On any night about one adult in fourteen failed to feed, and about one young bat in three.

blocks.caption: How the weight of a vampire bat falls after a full meal, and what a gift of 5 grams of blood does to a donor that has just fed and to a bat 48 hours from its last meal. A sketch with the pattern Wilkinson reported (fast loss at first, slow later), not his own data; the bat starves at the weight it reaches about 60 hours after a meal.

blocks.text: The shape of that curve holds Wilkinson's first clue. A bat that has just fed is losing weight quickly, mostly water. Take 5 grams of blood from it and it reaches the weight it would have had about 9 hours later: it is 9 hours nearer the starvation weight. A bat 48 hours from its last meal is losing weight slowly, so the same 5 grams put it back where it was about 28 hours earlier. A gift costs the giver much less time than it gives the receiver. That makes giving cheap, but it does not explain whom a bat should give to.

Biologists had two explanations for an animal helping another at a cost to itself. One is **kinship**: a relative shares many of your genes, so feeding a sister or a daughter helps copies of your genes survive. The other is **reciprocity**: help others and be helped in turn, which can work between unrelated animals as long as each remembers who helped and who refused. Reciprocity has a known weakness. A cheat that takes help but never gives saves its own food, and if nobody notices, cheats do better than givers and spread.

Wilkinson could test both because he knew, from years of records, which bats roosted together, and roughly how related they were, from the mothers and young he had followed and from inherited differences in proteins in small blood samples, which run in families much as blood groups do. Gifts went to relatives more often than if donors had picked roost-mates at random, and also to bats that spent a lot of time in the same roost, whether related or not. Then he kept a few adult bats in captivity, some of them unrelated and taken from two different roosts. Each night he kept one bat from feeding and watched who fed it. The bats fed roost-mates they knew, and a bat was more likely to be fed by one it had itself fed before.

blocks.caption: A model roost of thirty common vampires, six families of four adult females and a young bat, through a year of nights. Each bat feeds or fails at Wilkinson's rates and dies when it reaches the starvation weight, which a bat with no help reaches after two missed nights. A hungry bat begs; a gift moves both bats along the curve above. Rules: never share; kin only; pay back (feed your own young, and any bat that has fed you in the last 120 nights); everyone. Cheats take but never give.
blocks.task: Guess, then find the rule under which cheats lose

blocks.text: Without sharing, the arithmetic is grim. The chance of failing on two given nights in a row is 1 in 14 times 1 in 14, about 1 in 200. That is small for one night, but there are 365 nights in a year, and the chance of getting through all of them without such a pair is about 16%. Wilkinson worked it out from his rates: without sharing, about 82% of adults would die in a year. In the wild he found about a quarter of adults dying each year, from every cause together. In the figure's model nearly every honest bat that shares survives the year, because no bat in it dies of anything but hunger. Sharing within families keeps most bats alive, and feeds the cheats too, since a cheat's relatives feed it like any other relative. Sharing with everyone also lets cheats take and never pay. Only paying back starves them, because a cheat has never fed anyone, so once the roost's old debts run out no one owes it a meal.

So Wilkinson's answer to why and to whom was this: a vampire gives blood to relatives and to roost-mates it knows well, the bats most likely to feed it when it is the hungry one; and because a gift costs the giver far fewer hours than it gives, such exchanges leave both bats better off over a year. Gerald Carter, working with Wilkinson from about 2010, followed this further with captive colonies. Who had fed a bat before predicted who would feed it better than relatedness did. And a bat that had several regular donors was still fed well when one of them was taken away, while a bat that relied on one lost out. And in 2020 Carter and colleagues showed how strangers become partners: two unfamiliar bats put together begin by grooming each other, and only after the grooming has built up does one first bring up blood for the other.[^carter]

Vampires are three species out of about 1,480. Roughly seven bat species in ten eat insects and other small animals with jointed legs, as all fifteen of Washington's species do. The rest have found other food, and their faces show it. Nectar bats have long snouts and long tongues tipped with a brush of fine projections that sweep up nectar. Fruit bats have short, broad faces and strong jaws for crushing pulp. Insect-eaters have rows of small pointed teeth for cracking beetles and moths, and often large ears for hearing faint echoes.

A few eat larger animals. The greater bulldog bat of tropical America, *Noctilio leporinus*, hunts fish: it listens for the ripple where a fish's fin breaks the surface, then trails its long legs through the water and gaffs the fish with hooked claws. The fish-eating myotis, *Myotis vivesi*, lives on desert islands in the Gulf of California and flies out over the sea at night to snatch small fish and crustaceans from the waves. The fringe-lipped bat of Panama finds túngara frogs by listening to their mating calls, which Merlin Tuttle and Michael Ryan showed in 1981 by playing recorded calls from speakers that the bats flew down to.[^frogs] The spectral bat, with wings about a metre across, the largest bat in the Americas, eats birds, rodents and other bats.

blocks.caption: Eight bats to sort by what they eat, from a description of the face, teeth or feet. The clue is a description, not a photograph.

items.name: Little brown bat
items.clue: Small, with big ears and a plain snout; rows of tiny pointed teeth.
items.why: Sharp little teeth for cracking insects and big ears for faint echoes: the usual insect-eater's kit.

items.name: Lesser long-nosed bat
items.clue: A long, slender snout and a tongue that reaches far out, ending in a brush; small, weak teeth.
items.why: A long snout and a brush-tipped tongue reach into deep flowers for nectar; it hardly needs teeth.

items.name: Common vampire bat
items.clue: Two razor-edged upper front teeth, very few cheek teeth, and small pits around the nose.
items.why: Blade-like incisors cut the skin, the heat-sensing pits find warm blood, and there is nothing to chew.

items.name: Greater bulldog bat
items.clue: Huge feet on long legs, each toe with a long, curved, hooked claw; drooping lips.
items.why: Long legs and hooked claws gaff fish from the water's surface.

items.name: Jamaican fruit bat
items.clue: A short, broad face, a deep jaw, and wide flat-topped cheek teeth.
items.why: Wide grinding teeth and strong jaws crush fruit pulp.

items.name: Hoary bat
items.clue: Narrow pointed wings for fast flight in the open, short rounded ears, many small sharp teeth.
items.why: A fast open-air hunter of moths, with an insect-eater's teeth.

items.name: Spectral bat
items.clue: Wings a metre across, a large nose leaf, and long strong canines and slicing cheek teeth.
items.why: The biggest bat in the Americas, with a meat-eater's canines and slicing teeth, eats birds and rodents.

items.name: Egyptian fruit bat
items.clue: Large eyes, a face like a small dog's, no nose leaf, and broad grinding cheek teeth.
items.why: Big eyes for finding its way by sight, and grinding teeth for figs and other fruit.

blocks.text: Every spring, pregnant lesser long-nosed bats, *Leptonycteris yerbabuenae*, fly north from central and southern Mexico into the Sonoran Desert, some as far as southern Arizona, following the flowering of the giant cacti. In late summer they move into the mountain grasslands of southeastern Arizona, where the wild agaves bloom. An agave is a desert plant related to the yuccas. It lives for years as a rosette, a ring of thick, spiked leaves rising from one point at the ground, then puts all it has into one flowering stalk, sometimes taller than a house, and dies. The flowers at the top open in the evening, pale and sturdy, with a musty smell, and pour out nectar through the night.

The bat hovers, pushes its head into a cluster of flowers and laps, and comes away with its face and shoulders dusted with pollen. It visits many flowers on many plants in a night and may fly tens of kilometres between roost and feeding grounds. A plant that sets seed only once in its life needs pollen from a different plant, and a bat brings pollen from far away.[^outcross]

That raises a hard question. Hummingbirds drink nectar too, in the same deserts, and weigh a few grams, so a flower could feed one far more cheaply. Why should an agave make most of its nectar at night, enough to fuel a 25-gram bat, instead of making less by day for hummingbirds?

A hummingbird cannot do the night shift: it needs light to see and lets its body cool into torpor through the night. So the question is really why the agave flowers at night at all, when hummingbirds could do the job by day. Two reasons stand out. In a hot desert, nectar made during the day evaporates and costs water the plant can barely spare; at night the air is cool and the nectar stays put. And the bat is the better courier. Hummingbirds defend small territories, chasing others from the flowers nearby, so pollen they carry moves between neighbouring plants. Seeds mostly fall near their parent, so plants growing close together are often close relatives. A bat's furry face holds far more pollen than a beak, and it carries it kilometres. For a plant with one chance to set seed, a large courier that travels far is worth a large meal. Hummingbirds are not shut out: they, and bees, do feed at agave flowers that stay open into the morning, but most of the nectar is made for the night visitors.

Tequila is distilled from one agave, the blue agave of Jalisco. Growers do not let it flower: they cut out the young stalk so that the sugar stays in the swollen core of the plant, the piña, which they roast and ferment. They plant new fields from the shoots that sprout around the base of old plants, which are clones: genetically identical copies of their parent. Fields of these agaves are rarely pollinated by bats now, and are more open to disease, since what kills one plant can kill them all. Since 2016 a few distillers have sold "bat friendly" tequila, made by growers who let a small share of their plants flower for the bats.[^tequila]

In the tropics of the Americas, small fruit-eating bats such as the short-tailed fruit bats eat fruits full of tiny seeds: wild peppers, figs, nightshades, the trumpet tree *Cecropia*. A meal passes through a bat in as little as twenty minutes. The bat does not land to drop it. The seeds fall wherever the bat happens to be flying, much of the time over open ground between patches of forest.

Birds eat many of the same fruits, but a bird crosses open pasture only briefly, flies from tree to tree, and drops seeds where it perches. So when forest is cleared for pasture and then left, birds seed its edges and the ground under any lone tree, and the bats seed the middle. The plants that grow from those small seeds are **pioneers**, quick-growing plants that need open sun. They shade out the grass, give birds perches, and make room for forest trees to follow. In Chiapas, in southern Mexico, Rodrigo Medellín and Osiris Gaona caught seeds falling in traps in the 1990s and found that bats were dropping more seeds than birds into pastures and cut-over land.

blocks.caption: A strip of pasture 300 metres wide beside a forest, left alone after clearing, with seeds arriving each year from birds and from fruit bats. Play the years with and without the bats, and try leaving one tree standing. An illustrative model.
blocks.task: Play twenty years with the bats, then without them, and watch the far side

blocks.text: Fruit bats of the Old World (Africa, Asia, Europe and Australia), the flying foxes and their kin, do the same with bigger seeds and over longer distances. On some Pacific islands, such as Tonga, a flying fox is one of the last animals left big enough to swallow a large seed and carry it from one valley to the next. Where flying foxes are hunted out, trees with large seeds stop spreading.

blocks.caption: Five questions on what bats eat
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A vampire bat that has just fed gives 5 grams of blood to one that last fed 48 hours ago. How do the hours each gains or loses compare?
choices: The donor loses far fewer hours than the hungry bat gains, because a full bat loses weight fast and a hungry one slowly
Both change by the same number of hours, because the same 5 grams of blood moves between them
The donor loses more hours than the hungry bat gains, because a full bat burns blood faster
items.why: A bat that has just fed sheds water and weight quickly; one near starvation loses weight slowly. The same grams cover few hours near the top of the curve and many near the bottom.

items.ask: In a vampire roost where some bats take blood but never give, which sharing rule leaves those cheats worst off?
choices: Give only to bats that have fed you before
Give to any hungry roost-mate who asks
Give only to your own relatives
items.why: A cheat never feeds anyone, so under a rule of paying back no one owes it a meal. Giving to everyone, or to family, feeds cheats along with everyone else.

items.ask: A vampire bat that fails to feed one night in fourteen, with no help, is most likely to die how?
choices: By failing two nights in a row at some point, since it starves about 60 hours after a meal
By slowly losing condition over months of slightly too little blood each night
By eating too much on the nights it does feed and being unable to fly
items.why: Two failures in a row come about 1 night in 200, but over 365 nights most bats meet one. Wilkinson reckoned about 82% of adults would die in a year without sharing.

items.ask: Why does a wild agave in the desert flower at night and feed bats rather than hummingbirds?
choices: Night nectar loses less water, and a bat carries more pollen much further, to plants less likely to be related
Hummingbirds cannot reach the nectar of agave flowers because they hover too high above them
Bats need less nectar than hummingbirds, because they are cooler and spend the day asleep
items.why: Cool nights save the plant's water, and a bat with a pollen-dusted face visits plants far apart, while a hummingbird defends a few flowers close together.

items.ask: A cleared pasture is left alone next to a tropical forest. Which animals are most likely to start plants growing in its middle, far from any tree?
choices: Fruit bats, which drop small seeds in flight over open ground
Fruit-eating birds, which drop seeds mostly while perched in trees
Insect-eating bats, which carry seeds stuck to their fur
items.why: Birds seldom linger over open ground and mostly drop seeds where they perch. Fruit bats pass seeds within minutes of eating, wherever they are flying.

trpv1.title: One gene, two proteins
trpv1.text: Cells can cut the message copied from a gene in more than one way, a process called splicing, and so make different proteins from the same gene. In the vampire's heat-sensing nerve cells most of the TRPV1 made is a shorter form, which opens at a lower temperature than the full-length form the bat's other nerve cells make.

draculin.title: Medicine from spit
draculin.text: Draculin is one of several substances in vampire saliva that keep blood flowing; it blocks two of the proteins blood needs to clot. Another, a clot-dissolving enzyme later named desmoteplase, was tested as a treatment for strokes, though it failed to beat existing drugs in large trials.

carter.title: Raising the stakes
carter.text: Grooming costs little and is easy to stop if a partner does not groom back, so starting with grooming and moving on to blood lets two bats test each other before either risks a meal. Biologists call this way of building trust raising the stakes.

frogs.title: Calling for a mate, and dinner
frogs.text: Male túngara frogs make a whine followed by chucks. Females prefer calls with more chucks, but so do fringe-lipped bats, which find those calls easier to locate. So the frogs that attract the most mates also attract the most bats.

outcross.title: Why pollen from far away
outcross.text: Seeds from a plant fertilised by its own pollen, or by a close relative's, often grow weaker, because harmful versions of genes are more likely to be paired up. Pollen from a distant plant is less likely to be related.

tequila.title: Bats back off the list
tequila.text: The lesser long-nosed bat was listed as endangered in the United States in 1988 and in Mexico soon after. As its roosts were protected and its numbers recovered, the United States took it off the list in 2018, the first bat to be removed for recovery.
